issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette: Mark, a 53-year-old social worker from North America, has been grappling with the aftermath of a sexual assault that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event left an indelible mark on his psyche, and he now finds himself experiencing intense shame and terror whenever he recalls it. Each memory dredges up not just the physical pain but also the overwhelming sense of violation. "When I remember what happened," Mark admits, "the same terror floods me as if it were happening all over again." This fear is compounded by a profound feeling of shame that silences him; he knows what transpired but struggles to articulate his experience. The memory of the assault has fueled several maladaptive strategies in Mark's life. Most notably, he has started avoiding enclosed spaces and rumination about revenge. "I try not to be in small rooms or confined areas," he explains. "It feels like I can't escape if something goes wrong." This avoidance is driven by a deep-seated belief that being trapped will make him vulnerable again. Moreover, the thoughts of how to get even with his assailant consume much of his waking hours. The more he ruminates on revenge, the more entrenched his fear and anxiety become. Mark's threat perceptions are also heightened by his memories. Each time he remembers the assault, the terror is so intense that it triggers a persistent sense of danger in his daily life. "I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me," Mark confesses. This hyper-vigilance extends to avoiding unfamiliar places because he cannot assess their safety. The unpredictability of new environments exacerbates his fears, leading him to assume something bad is happening when delays occur. His avoidance behaviors have further reinforced his threat perceptions. For instance, whenever he steps into a crowded room or an enclosed space at work, the memory of the assault floods back with intense shame and terror. "I push those thoughts out of my mind," Mark says, acknowledging his efforts to suppress them. Yet, this suppression only serves to heighten his anxiety about potential threats. He believes that any delay in his daily routine could mean something is wrong, leading him to constantly monitor for signs of danger. Mark's avoidance has also strained his relationships with colleagues at work. His need to avoid enclosed spaces often means he misses important meetings or has to leave early. "I know it looks like I’m not taking my responsibilities seriously," Mark admits, feeling the weight of these actions on his professional life. Despite this awareness, he cannot shake off the pervasive fear that something bad will happen if he does not stick closely to familiar environments. What finally brought Mark to seek help was a particularly harrowing incident at work. During a mandatory meeting in an enclosed conference room, the memories overwhelmed him and he had to leave abruptly, leading to significant embarrassment and concern from his supervisor. "I’m afraid of becoming someone I don’t recognize," Mark says with a mixture of resignation and hope. He is desperate for relief from these overwhelming thoughts and fears that have taken over his life. In therapy, Mark hopes to find ways to process the memories without falling into cycles of avoidance and rumination. What frightens him most is the thought of never fully recovering and continuing to live in constant fear. His primary goal is to regain a sense of control and peace, so he can return to living a fulfilling life as a social worker and a husband.
